posts.title: A morning on the Wren
posts.excerpt: Skipper Tomas Varga takes the day boat Wren out from Berth 14 at dawn, bringing the morning catch back to the quay at Port Ellery before the kitchen begins its daily work.
posts.content:
The harbour bell has not yet rung when Tomas Varga unties the mooring lines at Berth 14. It is 05:30 on a Thursday morning in Port Ellery, and the water inside the stone breakwater is as flat as slate. The Wren, our small wooden day boat, hums quietly as its engine turns over in the cool morning air. Tomas coils the damp hemp lines on the wooden deck, checks the compass, and eases the bow out past the harbour beacon into open coastal water. There are no factory trawlers or deep-water dredging gear aboard; we fish strictly with hand lines and pots, working close to the rocky shelf that runs along our stretch of coastline.

At dawn, the first grey light breaks across the sea, turning the swell from dark charcoal to pale silver. Tomas sets the drift along the outer reef, watching the depth finder and reading the tidal current through the movement of the boat. Hand-line fishing requires patience, touch, and an intimate understanding of the seabed. On this morning, the lines come up heavy with silver-skinned mackerel and firm sea bream. Further south, along the sandy banks, the pots yield tender squid and a basket of seasonal crab, while the deeper drops produce several prime hake. Everything that comes over the gunwale is handled by hand, inspected immediately, and layered carefully into wooden crates with crushed ice.

There are no holding tanks on the Wren, and we never keep catch at sea overnight. What is caught in the first hours of daylight is what our guests will eat that evening at 7 Harbour Row. Tomas works steadily through the morning tide, keeping track of the weather and the clock. As mid-morning approaches, the lines are stowed, the deck is washed down with sea water, and the Wren turns back toward the harbour entrance. Behind us, the wake dissolves into the calm grey sea, and the stone roofs of Port Ellery slowly resolve through the coastal mist.

At 10:30 sharp, the Wren glides alongside the stone quay at Berth 14. Waiting on the cobbles are chef Inès Calder and Noor Haddad, wearing their flour-dusted aprons under heavy wool coats. Tomas cuts the engine and hands the crates up from the deck, calling out the morning tally: hake, mackerel, sea bream, squid, and crab. Inès kneels beside the first crate, checking the clear eyes and firm gills of the sea bream before nodding. Without delay, the entire landing has been carried across Harbour Row and into the kitchen prep room.

By 11:00, Noor Haddad is already at the wooden prep table, breaking down the fish while the heads and bones are rinsed for the six-hour stock-pot. At 15:00, Inès will take chalk to the dark slate board in the dining room, writing out the five courses of tonight's Boat Menu. When our guests sit down for the first seating at 18:00, the fish on their plates will carry the exact salt and cold of the morning tide. That direct unbroken line from Tomas's boat to our charcoal hearth is why Nagisa Grill exists.

posts.title: What we do with the rest of the fish
posts.excerpt: Roasted bones, a six-hour simmer and the broth that follows every service.
posts.content:
A whole fish is more than its fillets. When the morning catch reaches the kitchen, Noor Haddad breaks down each fish at 11:00, and the part that does not go on a plate is set aside at once: the bones, the heads, the trimmings. They are not stored for later in the week and they are not thrown away. They go into a steel tray and then into the oven.

The bones are roasted until they take on colour, then tipped into the big pot with water and a handful of vegetables. The stock simmers for six hours. It is never allowed to boil hard, because a hard boil clouds the broth and drives off the quiet flavour of the fish. A low flame, a skimming spoon and a clock on the wall are all the method there is.

By late afternoon the broth is ready to be strained. It is the base of the clear broth that sits under one course on the Boat Menu, and it is the reason the kitchen can serve a proper dinner on the days when the Wren stays in. On those days there is no new catch, so the shore plates and the stock-pot carry the evening.

Nothing about this is meant to sound like thrift for its own sake. It is simply what a kitchen that works with one boat has to do. If you only receive one catch each day, you learn what each part of the fish is good for, and you learn it in order: fillets for the grill, collars for the bar, bones for the stock.

The smaller trimmings have their own routine. Some are crisped for the shore plates, some are folded into the staff meal, and some go back to the quay for the harbour cats, who have their own opinions about the Wren. By the time the bar opens at 17:30, the kitchen smells of charcoal on one side and of broth on the other, and both are made from the same morning's work. The same logic applies to the evening. Once the last order is taken at 22:00, the stock-pot is lowered to its overnight flame, and the next day's pot begins with whatever the Wren lands in the morning.

posts.title: Four glasses for one boat
posts.excerpt: How the wine pairing for the Boat Menu is chosen, and why it is four glasses and not five.
posts.content:
The Boat Menu has five courses, and the pairing that goes with it has four glasses. Henrik Dahl, who looks after the zinc bar and the cellar, is asked about this more than almost anything else. The answer is not complicated: one of the five courses is the clear broth, and broth is better with nothing beside it.

Choosing wines for a menu that changes every day is a different job from choosing for a fixed one. Henrik does not know exactly what the Wren will land until the crates reach the quay at 10:30, so the pairing is built from a short list of wines that suit fish in general, then narrowed in the afternoon once the board is written at 15:00. Most of the bottles are crisp and mineral, with a few rounder whites held back for the whole fish grilled over charcoal.

The bar opens at 17:30, and early arrivals often start with a single glass and the shore plates. That is how many guests find out which style they like before the first seating at 18:00. Henrik pours small, tells you what is in the glass, and does not describe the wine in the language of perfume. If a glass tastes of salt, green apple and stone, that is what he says.

The pairing is optional and it is priced plainly at €42 for the four glasses, in addition to the €78 of the Boat Menu. Guests who prefer to choose by the glass can do so, and guests who would rather not drink wine are not asked twice. A good glass of water, still or sparkling, is also part of the table.

What the wine list shares with the rest of the restaurant is its scale. Nothing is there to impress, and nothing is stocked in the hope that someone will ask for it. The cellar is small because the kitchen is small, and the kitchen is small because there is only one boat. Four glasses is simply how many the evening needs. If you are unsure, ask at the bar before the first seating; Henrik would rather pour a taste than explain a label, and a taste costs nothing.

posts.title: How we hold a table
posts.excerpt: Four plain rules for booking a table: thirty days ahead, a deposit that comes off the bill, fifteen minutes of grace and a full refund until 15:00 the day before.
posts.content:
A table at Nagisa Grill is a promise made in both directions. We cook only as much fish as the Wren lands, and we prepare for the tables that are booked, so an empty chair at 18:00 is a piece of the morning's catch with nowhere to go. Everything about how we hold a table follows from that one fact.

The first rule is the simplest: book up to 30 days ahead, by the form or by email. Amara Osei keeps the table book by hand, and she reads every request herself. She replies with the date, the seating and the number of guests as she has written them down, so there is never any doubt about what has been agreed. Tables are for one to eight guests; for a larger party, please write to us first and she will plan the evening with the kitchen.

The second rule is the deposit. A deposit of €20 per guest holds the table, and it comes off the bill at the end of the evening. It is not a fee and it is not a penalty. It is how a small restaurant with one boat and one service shows that the table is real, and it lets the kitchen plan the fish without guessing.

The third rule is the quarter hour. We hold your table for 15 minutes after the seating time, at 18:00 or at 20:30. Trams are late and parking along the quay is never easy, and we would rather you arrived a little flushed than not at all. After the fifteen minutes the table goes back into the room, because the second seating has its own promise to keep.

The fourth rule is the way out. If your plans change, cancel by 15:00 the day before and the deposit is returned in full. That is the hour at which the board is written: by then Inès Calder has the morning's fish broken down in front of her, and she decides how many plates to build the evening around. A cancellation after that hour is a plate that has already been counted.

None of this is meant to feel strict. In the room, a held table feels like the opposite: a candle, a card with your name, a seat by the window if you asked for one, and nobody asking whether you are ready to order. The rules sit behind the evening so that the evening itself can be slow. When you arrive, everything has already been decided except the fish, and that is the part the sea chooses.

If you would like to be told when tables open, the Board arrives by email on Wednesday mornings, with the next two weeks of open seatings beside the notes from the boat.
